text: Christmas Eve, nineteen fourteen. Along parts of the Western Front, the guns fall silent. And nobody ordered it.
caption: Christmas Eve, 1914. Along parts of the Western Front, the guns fall silent. And nobody ordered it.

text: Five months into the First World War, British and German soldiers are dug into freezing, flooded trenches. Between them lies no man's land. In places, less than a hundred metres wide.
caption: Five months into the First World War, British and German soldiers are dug into freezing, flooded trenches. Between them lies no man's land. In places, less than 100 metres wide.

text: That night, near Ypres, British sentries spot lights along the German line. Small Christmas trees, glowing with candles.
Then the Germans begin to sing. Stille Nacht. Silent Night.
The British answer with carols of their own. Song by song, the two trenches take turns.
On Christmas morning, a few men climb out of their trenches. Unarmed.
Soon, soldiers from both sides are meeting in no man's land. They shake hands, and swap cigarettes, chocolate, buttons and beer.
And in some places, they even play football.
In some sectors, the truce lasts until Boxing Day. In a few, into the new year.
Commanders on both sides are furious. It will never happen on this scale again.
The war goes on for almost four more years, and claims millions of lives.
But for one Christmas, the men in the trenches chose peace, on their own.
